sections.title: Prototype, Experiment, and Learn 3D Printing
sections.intro: **From first-time prints to functional prototypes, our 3D printing lab is here to help.**

items.heading: What You Can Do in the 3D Printing Lab
items.text:
- **Print prototypes and functional parts** for engineering, robotics, and electronics projects.
- **Create cosplay props and costumes** that can be sanded, painted, and combined with laser-cut details.
- **Make replacement parts and brackets** for household fixes, shop jigs, and tools.
- **Design educational models** for classrooms, STEM demonstrations, and workshops.
- **Experiment with different materials** like PLA, PETG, and more as approved by the lab.
- **Combine 3D prints with laser-cut parts** for enclosures, signage, and multi-material builds.

items.heading: Equipment & Workflow
items.text:
Our 3D printing area is set up to make it easy to go from idea to printed part:

- Available Printers:
- AnyCubic Kobra S1, with 4 Filmanent AMS for **Multicolor** Printing
- Zortrax M200, 2X, **Easy and Reliable ABS** and Polycarbonate
- Elegoo OrangeStorm Giga, **HUGE 800x800x1000mm** Build Volume!
- Materials: PLA, PETG, ABS, HIPS, PCABS, AND MORE!!!
- Computer workstations for slicing and file preparation.
- Slicers - Prusa, Cura, Orca, ZSuite
- Tools for removal and post processing
- Guidance from members who print regularly

New to 3D printing? Start with a simple calibration cube or small project. We'll help you choose settings so you can get a successful first print.

items.heading: From Idea to 3D Printed Part: Basic Steps
items.text:
- **Start with a model.** Design your own part in CAD software or download a model from a site like Printables or Thingiverse.
- **Import into a slicer.** Use slicing software (like PrusaSlicer, Cura, or similar) to set layer height, infill, and supports.
- **Choose material and printer.** Pick an approved filament and an available printer profile.
- **Slice and save the file.** Export G-code to an SD card or send it using the recommended workflow for our printers.
- **Prepare the machine.** Check bed leveling, clean the build surface, and load filament.
- **Start the print and monitor the first layers.** The first layer tells you most of what you need to know about adhesion and leveling.
- **Remove, inspect, and iterate.** Once the print is done, remove it carefully, evaluate the results, and adjust settings for future runs.

items.heading: Digital Fabrication Workflow
items.text:
3D printing is even more powerful when you pair it with our laser cutters and other shop areas. Use the 3D printing lab to make complex shapes, then add laser-cut panels, inlays, or engraved details for a professional finish.

- 3D printed brackets with laser-cut acrylic panels.
- Electronics enclosures with engraved labels and cutouts.
- Cosplay armor that combines printed parts with foam and laser-cut accents.
- Signage with 3D printed lettering mounted on laser-cut backers.

items.heading: Next Steps After 3D Printing
items.text:
If you're ready to branch out beyond FDM printers, check out our other digital fabrication resources:

- [Laser cutter how-to guide](/how-to-use-a-laser-cutter) for safety and step-by-step operation.
- [Laser shop overview](/laser-shop) with details on Trotec laser capabilities.
- Woodworking, metalworking, and electronics areas for finishing and integrating your parts.

These tools together turn the makerspace into a full prototyping lab for personal projects, startups, and community teams.

items.heading: Ready to Explore the Lab?
items.text: Become a member of Kalamazoo Makerspace to access the 3D printing lab, laser cutters, and more.

items.heading: Do I need experience to use the 3D printers?
items.text: No prior experience is required. We'll help you with the basics of slicing, printer setup, and safe operation. 3D printing is beginner-friendly, and you'll learn a lot just by doing a few small projects.

items.heading: Is there required training like with the laser cutter?
items.text: We strongly recommend an orientation or informal training session so you understand how to level the bed, load filament, and recover from common issues like stringing or poor adhesion. Ask a volunteer or regular 3D printing user to walk you through the process.

items.heading: What software should I use for 3D printing?
items.text: Popular options include PrusaSlicer, Cura, and other FDM slicers. Many of these are free and well-documented. We can share printer profiles and recommended settings for our machines.

items.heading: Can I bring my own filament?
items.text: Yes, as long as it is a material approved for our printers (typically PLA or PETG). Check in with a volunteer before running unfamiliar materials so we can protect the equipment.

items.heading: How long do 3D prints take?
items.text: Print time depends on size, layer height, and infill. A small part might take under an hour, while large or detailed prints can run overnight. We'll help you estimate print times and plan accordingly.

items.heading: Can I 3D print parts and then laser cut matching pieces?
items.text: Absolutely. Many members design projects that combine 3D printed parts with laser-cut wood or acrylic. Read our [laser cutter guide](/how-to-use-a-laser-cutter) to learn how to safely use the laser shop.

items.heading: What are the most common 3D printing mistakes?
items.text: We see the same failures week after week: poor first-layer adhesion, wrong material selection, ignoring print orientation, and more. Read our guide on [common 3D printing failures](/how-to-3d-print-failures-we-see-every-week) to learn how to avoid them.

items.heading: Why do home 3D printers often sit unused?
items.text: Many home printers end up collecting dust due to calibration drift, maintenance burden, and lack of support. Learn [why makerspaces solve these problems](/how-to-why-most-3d-printers-sit-at-home-gathering-dust) through shared maintenance and collective knowledge.

items.heading: When should I NOT use 3D printing?
items.text: 3D printing has specific limitations in strength, surface finish, speed, and materials. Read our guide on [what 3D printing is bad at](/how-to-what-3d-printing-is-bad-at) to understand when laser cutting, CNC, or traditional tools are better choices.
